---
title: "Practical: water loss, leaf area and a mass balance"
---

## Question and study design

How does moving air relate to water loss from a hypothetical plant setup?
This classroom practical uses the [plant-water CSV](../data/plant-water.csv)
and [data dictionary](../data/README.md). No plant manipulation or apparatus
procedure is required. Use the course's actual laboratory protocol for any
future measurements.

Eight independently potted plants are randomised to still or moving air,
four per group. Each pot receives its setting independently; temperature,
humidity, illumination and position are controlled or balanced. Soil surfaces
are covered. Matched plant-free covered setups lose 0.10 g during the interval.
Assume that background applies to each experimental setup. These are supplied
simplifications, not observations you should claim to have verified.

## From a balance reading to a physiological quantity

An initial-to-final mass difference is a whole-setup measurement. In this
exercise we attribute corrected mass loss primarily to transpired water.
This is an approximation: real mass balances also require attention to leaks,
soil evaporation, material added/removed and other fluxes. A balance does not
measure a stomatal aperture or distinguish stomatal from cuticular water loss.

Calculate:

$$
 \Delta m_{corrected}=m_{initial}-m_{final}-\Delta m_{blank}
$$

$$
 E_{area}=\frac{1000\,\Delta m_{corrected}}{A\,(t/60)}.
$$

The mass values are in g, $A$ is the stated **one-sided** leaf area in
cm², and $t$ is in min. The result is mg cm⁻² h⁻¹. One-sided area is
a measurement convention; state it consistently rather than switching to
two-sided area midway through a comparison.

### Worked check

W01 loses 0.80 g. After a 0.10 g background correction, 0.70 g = 700 mg
is attributed to the plant. Its area is 50 cm² and the interval 0.5 h.
The area-specific loss is $700/(50\times0.5)=28$ mg cm⁻² h⁻¹.
The correction is subtracted once per setup, not once per leaf.

## Tasks

1. Identify the experimental unit, allocation groups and number of independent
   replicates. Why would one shared still-air cabinet and one shared moving-air
   cabinet weaken a treatment comparison?
2. Calculate corrected water loss and area-specific rate for all eight pots.
   Check W06 by hand before summarising the groups.
3. Draw an observation plot and calculate group means. Describe the size and
   variation of the difference in the given units.
4. Draw the path from soil water through root, xylem, leaf air spaces and
   stomata to the atmosphere. Mark where vapour diffusion occurs.
5. Explain how moving air can change the boundary layer at the leaf surface.
   Why might stomatal regulation prevent a simple proportional response to
   wind speed in a real plant?
6. Decide whether the data establish stomatal opening, photosynthetic rate or
   a species' drought tolerance. Explain what further measurements each claim
   would need.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

W06's observed 2.0 g loss becomes 1.9 g after correction, then 1900 mg.
Divide by 25 cm² h, not by 1500 cm² min while labelling the answer per hour.
:::

## Water potential: use the sign, not just the magnitude

For a short cell-level comparison neglect gravity and matric components and
use $\Psi_w=\Psi_s+\Psi_p$. A cell has solute potential −0.8 MPa and
pressure potential +0.3 MPa, so its water potential is −0.5 MPa. The adjacent
solution has water potential −0.2 MPa. Predict the initial direction of net
water movement across a permeable membrane, assuming the relevant solutes
do not freely cross. Explain why the movement slows as cell state changes.

Then consider an adjacent solution at −0.9 MPa. The direction reverses:
water moves from the higher water potential (less negative value) toward the
lower water potential. The two cases do not allow you to compute a flux
without hydraulic conductance, area and other information. Do not equate a
potential difference in MPa with a mass-loss rate.

## Completion check

Submit a labelled water-path diagram, a worked W06 calculation, the eight
rates and group means, and an interpretation linking gas exchange and water
conservation. Include one design limitation and your water-potential predictions.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Self-check

Still-air rates: 28, 36, 44 and 36 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹; moving-air rates: 60,
76, 92 and 76. Means are 36 and 76, a difference of 40. The cell in
−0.2 MPa solution initially gains water; in −0.9 MPa solution it loses water.
More water loss alone does not establish greater carbon gain or drought tolerance.
:::

For background, read the water-potential and transpiration sections in
[OpenStax: transport of water and solutes](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/30-5-transport-of-water-and-solutes-in-plants).
